title: How to Read a Landscape Contractor Quote (Line by Line)
seoTitle: How to Read a Landscaping Quote | Ontario
seoDescription: A complete landscaping quote breaks out at least 7 line items. Here is what each one means and what a vague quote is usually leaving out.
tldr: A complete landscaping quote breaks out at least 7 line items separately: excavation, base stone, geotextile, HPB bedding, paver or decking supply, labour, and equipment plus disposal. A lump-sum quote makes it impossible to compare bids or catch material substitutions during installation. In Ontario, permits are almost never included in a contractor’s quote unless they write it in explicitly — always ask.
intro:
Most homeowners in Ontario receive their first landscaping quote as a lump sum — a project name, a total, and a signature line on a single page. That format is not a quote; it is an invoice written before the work has started. A properly structured quote gives you enough detail to understand what you are actually buying, compare it line-for-line against other bids, and hold the contractor accountable if materials get swapped or a step gets skipped once the crew is on site.

After reviewing project quotes for interlocking patios, driveways, retaining walls, and TimberTech composite decks across Barrie, Innisfil, Oro-Medonte, and Springwater, the same omissions appear in low-ball proposals every time: excavation is “Included” with no depth or volume stated, the base description reads “gravel” rather than 3/4-inch clear stone over geotextile, and labour is bundled into one supply-and-install figure so you cannot see the actual breakdown. This guide walks through each line item in a credible contractor quote so you know what to look for and what to push back on before you sign.

sections.heading: What Every Landscaping Quote Should Break Out
sections.html:
A credible landscaping quote has at minimum 7 separate line items. If yours has fewer, ask the contractor to revise it before you compare it to other proposals. A quote that cannot be broken down cannot be fairly compared.

  • Excavation — depth in centimetres, estimated volume in cubic metres, and whether the material leaves the property or gets graded on-site.
  • Base stone — material type (3/4-inch clear stone, not simply “gravel”), number of lifts, and total volume.
  • Geotextile — square metres of filter fabric and the product grade; non-woven fabric is standard under paver bases in Simcoe County.
  • HPB bedding layer — the screeded layer directly under the pavers, specified separately from the base stone below it. Some contractors omit this entirely, which is a warning sign.
  • Paver or decking supply — specific product name, line, and thickness (for example, Permacon Lafitt or Unilock Beacon Hill Smooth 80mm), colour, quantity in square metres, and unit price.
  • Labour — scope and hours listed separately from material supply.
  • Equipment and disposal — bobcat time, plate compactor rental, and dump fees; these vary significantly by site access and soil type.

If your quote shows those 7 items with quantities and unit prices, you can verify the math, compare it to another bid, and catch substitutions before they happen. If it does not, ask for a revised version. A contractor who refuses to break it out is telling you something important about how they intend to run the job.

For more context on what separates a credible contractor from a low-ball one, see our guide on how to choose a landscaping contractor in Barrie.

sections.heading: The Excavation Line — Why It’s the Number That Makes or Breaks a Quote
sections.html:
Excavation is the single most variable cost on a landscaping project, and it is the line item most often hidden in a vague quote. The volume of material to remove depends on three factors: the target depth below finished grade, the square footage of the project, and what is already under the surface.

Barrie and much of Simcoe County sit on glacial till and clay-heavy soil. Clay does not drain — it holds water and amplifies freeze-thaw movement. Projects on a clay-dominant lot require excavation deep enough to place sufficient aggregate to manage drainage and limit frost-heave. Projects near Bayfield Street developments, Oro-Medonte subdivisions, or new builds in Springwater often hit fill material at unpredictable depths, which changes the excavation scope mid-project.

A vague quote that says “excavation included” is not accounting for any of this. A well-structured quote states the assumed depth in centimetres, an estimated volume in cubic metres, and a clause explaining what happens if actual conditions differ — for example, if the excavator hits 60cm of fill instead of native soil.

This is also the line item that reveals whether a cheap quote is actually cheap or just incomplete. Two proposals may both show the same paver product at the same supply price, but if one includes full excavation with haul-off and the other says “excavation TBD,” those are not comparable bids. The second one may carry a change order the moment the bobcat hits the ground.

Always ask: “If excavation runs deeper than your estimate, how will that be priced?” A contractor who has thought this through will give you a specific answer tied to a written change-order process.

sections.heading: Base Materials on a Quote — What ‘Gravel’ Actually Means
sections.html:
The base beneath your patio or driveway determines whether it stays flat for a decade or heaves and settles within a few seasons. Unfortunately, quotes often describe the base in a single vague word: “gravel.” In a credible quote, the base specification tells you three things: the material, the depth, and whether geotextile fabric is included.

The material matters. We use 3/4-inch clear stone — a washed, angular aggregate sourced through Carr Landscape Depot in Barrie that compacts tightly, drains freely, and resists lateral movement under freeze-thaw cycling. The word “gravel” can mean any number of things: crusher run, crusher fines, 7/8-inch round stone, or recycled asphalt granular. Each performs differently. Clear stone drains; crusher fines hold water. The right material for Simcoe County winters is specified clearly in a quote that knows what it is doing.

Geotextile fabric should appear as a separate line item in every quote. The fabric is installed on the native soil before the base stone goes in, separating the base from the subgrade so fines do not migrate up and contaminate the stone layer over time. If a quote does not list geotextile, ask where it is — or assume it is not planned.

The HPB (High-Performance Bedding) layer is the screeded layer pavers sit on directly. It is a different product and serves a different function from the base stone. A quote that specifies only “base gravel” with no mention of HPB is describing an incomplete installation. Base depth is project-specific and varies by soil type, drainage conditions, and the intended use of the surface. Any contractor claiming a single universal depth across all projects is not accounting for the soil variability common across Simcoe County.

Base material specifications also affect how a quote handles future repairs. If the spec is in writing, there is no dispute about what was installed if a section needs to be lifted and relevelled in year 5.

sections.heading: Labour vs. Supply — Why the Split Matters When Comparing Bids
sections.html:
When a contractor lists a single line item — “supply and install, 300 sq ft patio” — it is impossible to verify whether the material cost is reasonable or whether the labour rate is competitive. The lump-sum format exists in part because it prevents comparison. When labour and supply are separated, you can spot the contractor who is marking up materials heavily to compensate for a lower labour rate, or the one quoting inexpensive stone to hit a price point before substituting on-site.

In a detailed quote, the supply line includes: material cost from the supplier, delivery charges, and any applicable taxes on goods. The labour line includes: excavation crew hours, base installation, paver setting, cutting, polymeric sand application, and final plate-compaction passes. Some contractors break labour out further into excavation labour and installation labour, which is useful when comparing crews with different equipment setups.

The ratio between labour and supply shifts depending on project complexity. A simple rectangular patio with a single running-bond pattern uses far less cutting labour than a curved design with a soldier-course border and a soldier inset at the steps. If you are comparing two bids, ask both contractors to show you the split. The contractor unwilling to do it may be protecting a margin the other contractor does not carry.

Equipment and disposal is worth checking separately. Hauling excavated material off a Barrie or Innisfil property adds real cost: dump fees, truck rental or bobcat time, and driver hours. A quote that buries this in a lump sum may be planning to grade the material on-site instead of removing it, which can create drainage issues on a clay-heavy lot. Ask specifically: “Is excavated material being removed from the property or redistributed?”

sections.heading: Red Flags — What a Low Quote Is Usually Leaving Out
sections.html:
A quote that comes in 20 to 30 per cent below every other bid is not necessarily a better deal. In most cases, one or more of these items has been left out or underspecified:

  • No excavation depth stated. Base depth is project-specific — it varies by soil, use, and drainage conditions. A quote with no depth specification cannot be held to anything if the base turns out shallow after the job is complete.
  • No geotextile listed. Skipping the fabric saves a small amount on materials but costs considerably more in settlement over the first several freeze-thaw cycles on a Barrie clay lot. This is one of the most common omissions in low proposals.
  • Generic paver specification. “Interlocking stone” or “paver product TBC” is not a specification. The product affects both aesthetics and long-term performance. An 80mm Techo-Bloc Blu paver behaves differently under heavy vehicle traffic than a 60mm residential patio unit. If the product is not named, the contractor can substitute without consequence.
  • No disposal line. Excavated clay from a Barrie lot weighs considerably more than the volume suggests. Disposal is a real cost. If it is not on the quote, expect it as a change order once the bobcat is on-site.
  • HST not addressed. Ontario HST is 13% and must be charged on taxable supplies by most registered contractors. A quote that says “HST included” on a large project is unusual — always confirm whether the total shown is before or after tax before you compare figures.

For a broader breakdown of costs that often appear after a low-ball quote is accepted, see our resource on hidden costs in cheap landscaping. The same gaps that make a quote look cheap on paper are usually the same ones that drive up the final invoice.

sections.heading: Questions to Ask Before You Sign a Landscaping Contract
sections.html:
No quote is complete until you have asked a few direct questions. These are worth raising before you agree to anything:

What happens if excavation goes deeper than the quote assumes? The honest answer will reference a price-per-extra-centimetre or a formal written change-order process. “We’ll figure it out” is not a sufficient answer on a Simcoe County clay site.

Are the base material specifications in writing? Ask for the specific materials — 3/4-inch clear stone over geotextile with HPB bedding — to appear in the signed contract, not just in conversation. If it is not in writing before work starts, you have no recourse if something cheaper goes in.

Who is your material supplier? Knowing the supplier tells you whether you can verify the product. We source pavers and base materials from Carr Landscape Depot in Barrie. You can confirm that the product exists and matches the spec before work begins.

Is HST included or excluded in the total? Always confirm this before comparing totals between contractors. A 13% difference can look like a price difference when it is really a tax-presentation difference.

What is the payment schedule? A deposit in the range of 20 to 30 per cent is typical for a project in this market. Requests for more than half the total upfront on a large project are not standard practice.

Are permits our responsibility or yours? Permits for retaining walls above a certain height, drainage modifications, or structures near the property line are almost always the homeowner’s responsibility unless a contractor explicitly writes it into scope. Never assume permits are covered.

faqs.question: What is a normal payment schedule for a landscaping project in Ontario?
faqs.answer: A deposit of 20 to 30 per cent is typical for projects in Barrie and Simcoe County, with progress payments tied to defined milestones such as base completion and paver setting, and a final payment on completion. Requiring more than half the total before work begins is not standard. Requiring full payment before the job starts is a warning sign worth investigating before you sign.

faqs.question: Should HST be included in a landscaping quote in Ontario?
faqs.answer: Ontario HST is 13% and must be collected by most registered contractors on taxable supplies. A well-structured quote shows the total before HST with HST listed as a separate line. If a quote says HST included, confirm this in writing before comparing it to other bids — what looks like a price difference between two proposals is sometimes just a difference in how HST is presented.

faqs.question: What does supply and install mean on a landscaping quote?
faqs.answer: Supply and install means the contractor is providing both materials and labour as a single bundled price. The problem is that this format makes it difficult to compare bids, verify material costs, or understand what changes if one element of the scope shifts. Whenever possible, ask the contractor to separate the supply cost from the labour cost so you are comparing equivalent breakdowns.

faqs.question: Can a contractor change the price after signing a landscaping quote in Ontario?
faqs.answer: A signed quote is a contract, and the total should not change without a written change order that you approve before the work is done. Price changes are typically triggered by unforeseen site conditions such as deeper excavation, unexpected fill material, or scope additions you request. Any contractor who adjusts pricing without a written and signed change order is operating outside standard industry practice.

faqs.question: What base material should be under an interlocking patio in Barrie?
faqs.answer: We use compacted 3/4-inch clear stone over geotextile fabric, with a screeded HPB (High-Performance Bedding) layer directly under the pavers. Base depth is project-specific and depends on soil type, drainage, and use — Barrie’s clay-heavy soil requires careful drainage management to prevent freeze-thaw heaving. Any quote that specifies only “gravel” without naming the material type and stating the depth is incomplete.

faqs.question: How do I compare two landscaping quotes that are very different in price?
faqs.answer: Start by confirming both quotes are describing the same scope: the same square metres, the same material specs, and the same excavation assumptions. Then check whether each one breaks out excavation, base stone, geotextile, bedding, paver supply, labour, and disposal separately. A lower total that omits disposal, geotextile, or HPB bedding is not a comparable bid — it is a quote for different work, and the gap will show up as change orders once the job is underway.

faqs.question: Do landscaping contractors in Ontario include permits in their quotes?
faqs.answer: Permits for retaining walls above a certain height, drainage modifications, and structures near property lines are almost always the homeowner’s responsibility in Ontario. A contractor may assist with applications as a service, but the permit obligation belongs to the property owner by default. Always ask specifically whether permits are included in scope — never assume they are covered unless it is written into the contract.
